implementation_notes: Grand Central Dispatch is the platform's pool: DispatchQueue.global() hands out work that 'executes on a pool of threads managed by the system' (the documented model), async { } enqueues without blocking, and DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform(iterations:execute:) fans a fixed number of iterations across the pool, returning only when all of them finish - the closest thing to a bounded parallel-for. You never create threads or size a pool: the system owns it, QoS classes prioritise work, DispatchGroup coordinates completion, and the docs explicitly warn that blocking inside concurrent blocks makes the system create more threads to compensate.
pitfalls: Blocking calls inside a concurrent dispatch block make the system spawn compensating threads; the docs' 'avoiding excessive thread creation' warning is about exactly this.
Global queues are shared with the rest of the app: heavy default-QoS work delays unrelated tasks, so choose the QoS deliberately.
There is no exact thread count to tune - the system decides the pool size, and concurrentPerform exists to bound the fan-out instead.

variants.name: GCD global concurrent queue / concurrentPerform

variants.name: OperationQueue with maxConcurrentOperationCount
variants.implementation_notes: OperationQueue is an explicit pool with a scheduling policy: maxConcurrentOperationCount caps how many operations run concurrently, dependencies order them, isSuspended pauses dispatch, and waitUntilAllOperationsAreFinished()/Progress expose completion while the queue runs operations on the system's dispatch pools underneath. Use it when tasks need dependencies, priorities, observability or cancellation semantics rather than raw parallelism - it is a policy layer over GCD, not a private thread pool, so it is the direct analogue of the classic pool manager.
pitfalls: The queue retains operations until they finish and a suspended queue retains them too, so a suspended queue with pending work looks like a leak.
cancel() only sets a flag: the operation body must check isCancelled and stop, and cancelling makes an operation ignore its dependencies and start as soon as possible (documented).
Operations that block occupy one of the concurrent slots for their whole duration, exactly like pool workers.

variants.name: Structured concurrency (TaskGroup)
variants.idiom_name: withTaskGroup + child tasks on the cooperative pool
variants.implementation_notes: Swift's concurrency model replaces the explicit pool in async code: child tasks added to a TaskGroup run on the runtime's cooperative pool, the group always awaits all of them before returning, and cancellation propagates from the parent (cancelAll() plus cooperative isCancelled checks) instead of through a thread API. Bounded fan-out is expressed as a window of awaited tasks rather than a pool size, and because the executor is cooperative, blocking a task blocks a thread for every task multiplexed on it - so this form suits async workloads, while CPU-bound synchronous fan-out still fits GCD/concurrentPerform.
variants.code_sketch:
await withTaskGroup(of: Result.self) { group in
    for job in jobs { group.addTask { await handle(job) } }   // cooperative pool
    for await result in group { collect(result) }             // always awaits all
}
pitfalls: Never block (sleep, synchronous I/O, locks) inside a task: the cooperative pool has roughly as many threads as cores.
A task group always waits for all child tasks even after an early return (documented) - use cancelAll() plus cooperative checks to stop early.
Cancellation is cooperative: ignore isCancelled and the work keeps running to completion.
